title: Social Determinants of Health

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Two students are told to practice basketball daily. One has a hoop in the driveway; the other walks twenty minutes to a court with a bent rim. If the second practices less, the honest explanation is not that she cares less - her surroundings made the same instruction harder to follow. Social determinants of health apply that logic to health: the housing, schooling, work, and neighborhood conditions surrounding a person, which make healthy living easier or harder before anyone makes a single choice. Notice what the definition leaves out: it is not about genes, and it is not about willpower.

### Question 2

Think of the five domains as five labeled bins that public health workers use to sort everything that shapes health. One bin holds money and work, one holds school and reading skills, one holds getting and using medical care, one holds the people and relationships around you, and one holds the physical place itself - the buses, sidewalks, water, and buildings. That last bin is called neighborhood and built environment. "Built" simply means the parts humans constructed, as opposed to anything happening inside your body. If a factor lives inside the body, it does not go in any of these bins.

### Question 3

These four terms sound similar but answer four different questions. "Is there a full grocery store within reach?" is the food desert question, and it is about geography. "Are the nearby options mostly fried and packaged?" is the food swamp question, about what fills that geography. "Can my household reliably afford enough food this month, or am I skipping meals to stretch it?" is food insecurity, about resources and uncertainty. "Is this person's body actually short on nutrients?" is undernutrition, about physiology. The stem asked about money and uncertainty, so the answer is food insecurity.

### Question 4

Chronic disease management is less one big decision than a chain of small, on-time events: a visit every three months, a refill every month, a lab draw twice a year. Every link in that chain requires a trip. When the nearest clinic is 45 minutes away and no bus exists, the chain breaks at whichever link lands on a week with no working car or no one to cover a shift. Nothing about the biology changed - what changed is how many links actually happened. A year later that shows up as a higher A1C, and the cause is the missing trips, not missing motivation.

### Question 5

Picture people repeatedly falling into a river and being swept downstream. You can stand at the bottom pulling them out one at a time - that is the emergency visit, the inhaler, the teaching session - and that work saves lives, so it is not optional. Or you can walk to the top and repair the broken railing they keep falling through. Repairing the railing is "upstream." The moldy apartment is that railing here: while it stays broken, the same children arrive in the water again next winter. The test for upstream is simple - does this change stop new cases from being generated?

### Question 6

Imagine a school whose heating system has failed. "This building is cold" is a statement about the whole school - that is the determinant. "Maya is shivering at her desk and needs a coat right now" is a statement about one student - that is the health-related social need. Both are true, and you hand Maya the coat immediately; screening and referral exist precisely for that. But distributing coats indefinitely is not the same as repairing the furnace, and a program that only counts coats will report success while the building stays cold. Competent public health does both and stays clear about which one it is doing.

### Question 7

Picture a staircase where each step up brings slightly cleaner air. The bottom step is worst, but step four is also measurably better than step three, and step nine better than step eight - the improvement keeps going all the way up. That steady, step-by-step change is what "gradient" means, and it is the opposite of a cliff edge with one bad side and one good side. So the useful question about socioeconomic position is never just "poor or not poor" but "which step," because a policy that only lifts people just over a poverty line leaves the rest of the staircase exactly as it was.

### Question 8

Reading in general and reading a medicine label are not the same skill. Plenty of adults who finish the newspaper without trouble will stall on "take one tablet by mouth twice daily as needed for pain" beside a second bottle warning against taking it with dairy - that is health words, health numbers, and health timing all at once. Healthy People 2030 sorts that particular struggle into the bin about getting and using health care, because the care system is the one handing over the information and is responsible for making it usable: plain-language labels, a pharmacist who explains, a nurse who asks you to say it back in your own words. The school-and-education bin holds general reading and writing skill instead, and the government's own page is explicit that plain reading skill and health literacy are two different things.

### Question 9

A chart works like a form with labeled fields. If housing instability only ever appears as a sentence inside a progress note, no query can count it, so the organization never learns that a third of its patients are unstably housed - the information exists but is invisible to every report. Z codes give that fact its own field. Once it is in a field it can be counted, and once counted it can be argued from: a clinic can justify hiring a housing navigator with data instead of impressions. The code is not diagnosing a disease; it is recording a circumstance.

### Question 10

If you keep getting flat tires because one street is covered in broken glass, you can become an expert at patching tubes, or you can call the people whose actual job is street cleaning. Health systems are excellent at patching. What they cannot do is issue a housing citation, change a zoning rule, or file a tenant complaint - other institutions hold those tools by law. Working with legal aid and the housing authority means borrowing tools your own toolbox does not contain. That borrowing across fields is what "cross-sector" means, and handing someone a phone number is not the same as it.

### Question 11

Suppose a car will not start and you replace the battery. If the fuel line is also clogged and the starter is worn, the car still will not start - and that does not prove the battery was irrelevant. It proves the battery was one of three things wrong. The free clinic is the new battery: it genuinely solved "I cannot afford to see anyone." The clogged fuel line is the corner store with no fresh produce and no place to store insulin. The worn starter is the apartment you keep having to leave and the bus that does not reach the pharmacy. Fix one, get one part of the result.

### Question 12

Think of a card game. The rules setting who is dealt how many cards are the structural part - they determine what hand each player starts with. The cards actually in your hand, and how tense you feel playing them, are the intermediary part. Helping someone play a weak hand better is worthwhile and you should do it. But if the same players are dealt two cards while others are dealt seven, hand after hand comes out lopsided no matter how skillfully anyone plays, until the dealing rules change. Policies on income, schooling, and political power are those dealing rules.
